ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The 6 April 2009 Lâ€™Aquila earthquake struck a portion of the Central Apennines that was believed to be especially well known from a seismotectonic point of view. The region is undergoing SW-NE active extension and is affected by strong earthquakes with magnitude up to 7.0 (CPTI Working Group, 2004).
Through the years several investigators have mapped the numerous active faults of the region. These faults are mostly extensional and SW-dipping, but for many of them no consensus exists concerning state of activity and hierarchical level (i.e. the relevance for seismic hazard).
Similarly to the mapped surface faults, all the different seismogenic sources proposed in the literature prior to the Lâ€™Aquila earthquake dip to the SW and display extensional kinematics; the geometric and dimensional relationships of each seismogenic source with the overlying surface faults, however, has been the object of a lively debate for at least a decade.
The San Pio delle Camere Fault has been recognized as active by several articles by independent groups (e.g. Bosi, 1975; Bagnaia et al., 1989; Vezzani and Ghisetti, 1998; ITHACA Working Group, 2000; Morewood and Roberts, 2000; Pizzi et al., 2002; Roberts and Michetti, 2004; Servizio Geologico d'Italia, 2006).
This Source is located with a left en-echelon step at the south-eastern edge of the seismogenic source of the 6 April 2009 Lâ€™Aquila earthquake. Its location and geometry was constrained by field work and geomorphic analysis on the basin running from Barisciano to Civitaretenga-Navelli, where converging morphotectonic, geological and structural evidence point to the presence of an active large SW-dipping normal fault (Di Bucci et al., 2011a).
These indications include (in descending order of importance):
1) a N130Â° elongated, ca. 15 km long, actively subsiding depression named San Pio basin, filled by Pleistocene and Holocene fluvial and lacustrine deposits;
2) a characteristic drainage pattern and architecture of deposits suggesting that the basin is controlled by a large and relatively deep fault;
3) a weakly uplifting range, bounding the basin and parallel to it;
4) a barely visible, SW dipping, normal fault system, formed by a set of fractures and of subtle, 60Â°-70Â° dipping, synthetic and antithetic normal faults, located between the basin and the range and affecting Recent-to-Present deposits.
These lines of evidence altogether are believed to be the result of sustained slip over a seismogenic fault adjacent to the 6 April rupture. Overall the San Pio basin makes a good candidate for being the long-term expression of a seismogenic fault comparable to the source of the 6 April 2009 earthquake. It has an active, marshy depocenter located in its central part. In literature, a faintly visible, SW-dipping, normal fault system is hypothesized between the basin and the range, and interpreted as reactivated during the Pleistocene and currently active.
Messina et al. (2011) raised a number of issues that would invalidate the conclusions of the article of Di Bucci et al. (2011a) on the existence and activity of the San Pio delle Camere Source. In their response, Di Bucci et al. (2011b) showed recent lacustrine silts tilted toward the fault depocentre, and other lines of geological and geomorphological evidence supporting the recent activity of the source.
According to the current historical catalogue, over the past 7 centuries the region hit by the 2009 earthquake sequence and that located south-east of Lâ€™Aquila has been hit by three significant shocks:
- 1315, 3 December (M 5.6; from CPTI11), a rather obscure earthquake that is known to have generically damaged "the Aquila castles";
- 1461, 27 November (M 6.4; from CPTI11), similar in strength to the 2009 but difficult to locate precisely due to the small number of intensity data, possibly reflecting an overlap with the effects of the 1456 earthquake, on the northern slope of the Maiella Massif;
- 1762, 6 October (M 6.0; from CPTI11), that struck all villages around San Pio delle Camere.
The 1461 and 1762 damage distributions are rather similar to that of the 2009 earthquake but shifted towards the southeast by a few km. Overall the accuracy of the available locations does not allow any of these earthquakes to be assigned confidently to the 6 April or to nearby sources (e.g. San Pio delle Camere). However, based on the analysis of historical intensity reports, Tertulliani et al. (2010) suggested that both the M 6.4, 1461 and the M 6.0, 1762 earthquakes were generated by the same source as the 2009 event, or by an antithetic structure cutting through the same seismogenic volume. Palaeoseismological studies across different segments of the Paganica and San Demetrio Faults returned different results: on the one hand Galli et al. (2010; 2011) contended that the Paganica Fault ruptured during the 1461 and the 2 February 1703 (M 6.7) earthquakes, while on the other hand Cinti et al. (2011) recognised five paleo-events which include the 1461 but not the 1703 earthquake.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Is the San Pio delle Camere Fault the seismogenic source of the 1762 earthquake? Or is it the source of the 1461 earthquake?
2) Which are the structural and dynamic relationships among the San Pio delle Camere Fault and the nearby sources and active faults (e.g. 6 april 2009 to the NW; Middle Aterno Valley fault system to the SSE)?
